subject: Anatomy
summary: The trachea is a 10‑12 cm cartilaginous tube that conducts air from larynx to main bronchi. Its rigidity, mucosal lining and blood supply protect the airway and influence many emergency presentations.

sections.p: The trachea is a midline respiratory conduit extending from the cricoid cartilage (C6) to the carina at T4‑T5. It is supported by C‑shaped hyaline cartilage rings and a posterior membranous wall.
b: Length ~10‑12 cm, diameter ~2 cm in adults
15‑20 incomplete cartilage rings
Mucosa contains ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells

sections.p: It lies anterior to the esophagus, within the visceral (pretracheal) fascia, and is slightly right‑deviated in the thorax.
b: Upper border: inferior to cricoid cartilage
Lower border: bifurcates into right/left main bronchi at the carina
Posterior wall: smooth muscle (trachealis) allows slight diameter change

sections.p: In the neck, the trachea is surrounded by thyroid, parathyroids, and recurrent laryngeal nerves; in the thorax, it contacts the aortic arch and superior vena cava.
b: Lateral: thyroid lobes (upper), brachiocephalic vessels (mid)
Posterior: esophagus
Superior: larynx and cricoid cartilage

sections.p: Arterial blood comes from inferior thyroid arteries (cervical) and bronchial arteries (thoracic). Venous drainage follows the thyroid and bronchial veins to the brachiocephalic veins.
b: Cervical segment: inferior thyroid artery branches
Thoracic segment: bronchial arteries from thoracic aorta

sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the recurrent laryngeal nerves (branch of vagus) and the vagus itself; autonomic fibers regulate mucosal secretions.
b: Afferent cough reflex via vagus
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from vagus

sections.p: Provides a rigid, protected airway, humidifies inspired air, and clears secretions via ciliary action and cough reflex.
b: Cough reflex triggered by irritant receptors in tracheal mucosa
Trachealis muscle adjusts lumen during coughing

sections.p: Trauma, infection, or obstruction of the trachea can cause life‑threatening airway compromise. Recognising patterns such as deviated trachea, neck vein distension, or absent breath sounds guides emergency care.
b: Tension pneumothorax: deviated trachea away, hypotension, distended neck veins
Tracheal deviation from large pleural effusion or mass pushes airway opposite side
Traumatic tracheal rupture: subcutaneous emphysema, hoarseness, air leak

t.b: Does the trachea deviate and is there a pneumothorax? → Confirms tension pneumothorax; immediate needle decompression needed
Is there tracheal wall disruption or mediastinal mass? → Guides surgical repair or oncologic work‑up
Is there intraluminal obstruction (foreign body, tumor, severe edema)? → Allows direct visualization and therapeutic removal

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Trachea is normally midline; deviation signals space‑occupying process or pressure imbalance
C‑shaped rings open posteriorly; injury often tears membranous wall
Cough reflex depends on vagal afferents; loss suggests high cervical spinal injury

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden tracheal deviation with hypotension (possible tension pneumothorax)
Severe dyspnoea with stridor and palpable neck mass (possible airway obstruction)
Rapidly worsening neck swelling with subcutaneous emphysema (possible tracheal rupture)

faq.q: Why does the trachea deviate in a tension pneumothorax?
faq.a: Air accumulation raises intrapleural pressure, pushing the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side.

faq.q: What protects the trachea from collapsing during coughing?
faq.a: The C‑shaped cartilage rings keep the lumen open; the posterior membranous wall can expand.

faq.q: How is the cough reflex initiated?
faq.a: Irritant receptors in the tracheal mucosa send afferent signals via the vagus to the medulla, triggering a coordinated expiratory effort.

exam: Explain how tracheal deviation helps differentiate tension pneumothorax from large pleural effusion.
Describe the blood supply to the cervical and thoracic portions of the trachea and its clinical relevance in surgery.
List three emergency conditions that present with a deviated trachea and the immediate management steps.
